text.en: In 166, men claiming to be envoys of the ruler of Rome — probably Marcus Aurelius — reached China. At the time, Rome was in the grip of the Antonine Plague.
Among the first Christian states were Armenia (traditionally 301) and Aksum in Ethiopia (around 330). Rome merely legalized Christianity in 313.
In January 378, a party from Teotihuacan arrived at the Maya city of Tikal, about 1,000 km away. Soon the city had a new ruler.
Twenty-three years after the Western Roman Empire fell, India's Aryabhata wrote that the sky only appears to move — it is the Earth that rotates.
A little over a century after Vesuvius buried Pompeii, across the ocean in Teotihuacan the Pyramid of the Sun rose — one of the largest pyramids in the world.
A vomitorium was not a room where Romans threw up at feasts. It was a passage through which an amphitheatre crowd could 'spew forth' quickly after the show, from Latin vomere, 'to spew'.

Gladiators were nicknamed hordearii, 'barley-eaters'. They lived on a nearly vegetarian diet of barley, beans and dried fruit thought to build strength, while legionaries got barley instead of wheat only as a punishment.
The Colosseum opened a year after Pompeii was buried, under the same emperor. Titus came to the throne in the summer of 79, Vesuvius erupted that same year, and in 80 he inaugurated the amphitheatre.

Roman concrete can heal its own cracks. A 2023 study found that lime lumps in the mortar, long dismissed as sloppy mixing, react with seeping water and seal cracks with fresh calcium carbonate crystals.

The last Western emperor bore the names of Rome's founder and its first emperor: Romulus Augustus. Romans called the boy Augustulus, 'little Augustus'. Odoacer spared him and sent him to live out his days in a castle in Campania.

The earliest record of Christmas as a feast on 25 December is in a Roman almanac of 354. The same 'Chronograph' lists the popes of Rome and the schedule of public games, with the number of chariot races.

Aksum's tallest stele, 33 metres high, probably collapsed as it was being raised and still lies broken. The last one erected was likely the 21-metre stele of King Ezana, under whom Aksum became Christian.
The coins of the Kushan king Kanishka show gods from four civilisations: Greek, Iranian, Indian and even the Sumero-Elamite goddess Nana. Among them is the Buddha, labelled in Greek letters: ΒΟΔΔΟ.
Pliny the Elder complained of gold draining east: India, China and Arabia, he wrote, take a hundred million sesterces from the empire every year. 'That is what our luxuries and women cost us.'
In AD 2 China held a census and counted 57,671,400 people in 12,366,470 households: the oldest surviving nationwide census of China, accurate to the individual.
AD 9 shook both great empires of Eurasia. Rome lost three legions in the Teutoburg Forest, and in China Wang Mang overthrew the Han and proclaimed his own Xin dynasty.

Cuneiform was still being written shortly before Pompeii was buried. The last known cuneiform tablet, an astronomical text, dates to about AD 75 — four years before Vesuvius erupted — when the script was over 3,200 years old.
Roman public latrines had a sponge on a stick, the tersorium, instead of toilet paper. It was rinsed in a channel of water or vinegar running at the users’ feet, and was probably shared.

According to Pliny the Elder, Emperor Nero watched gladiator fights through an emerald. Whether it was a lens or just a sunshade is still debated, but spectacles would not appear for another 1,200 years.
Caligula never made his horse a consul. Suetonius says only that Incitatus had a marble stall and an ivory manger, and that the emperor was “said to have planned” to make him consul.
Rome paid the Goths in pepper. In 408 Alaric demanded 5,000 pounds of gold, 30,000 of silver and 3,000 of pepper to lift his siege. Two years later he took the city anyway.
The first vending machine sold holy water. Hero of Alexandria described a temple device in which a coin fell onto a lever that opened a valve and released a measured squirt of water.
An ancient temple could have automatic doors. Hero described how a fire on the altar heated air that pushed water into a counterweight bucket, swinging the doors open as if by divine will.

The Romans used nanotechnology without knowing it. The 4th-century Lycurgus Cup is green in reflected light and red when lit from within, thanks to gold and silver particles just tens of nanometres wide.

The Romans left over a hundred mysterious bronze dodecahedra and not a single word about what they were for. They have been called rangefinders, calendars, candlesticks and even tools for knitting gloves.

In 138 Zhang Heng's seismoscope in Luoyang signalled an earthquake that nobody had felt. The court was sceptical, until a messenger arrived days later: there had indeed been a quake in distant Longxi.

Nero could not have fiddled while Rome burned: the violin was invented in the 16th century. According to Tacitus he was at Antium when the fire broke out, and on returning opened his gardens to the homeless.
